To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
wheat growth and yield are sensitive to changes in air temperature and ambient CO2 concentration.
the direct effects of elevated CO, on wheat photosynthesis and transpira- tion may be offset by the indirect effects on crop growth through increased water use efficiency and reduced water stress.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and testing of a model that simulates the direct responses of wheat canopy photosynthesis and stomatal conductance to ambient CO2 concentration, and the responses of wheat crop growth to water and nitrogen stresses.
developing a wheat growth model to simulate the effects of increased air temperature and CO2 concentration, and rainfall on wheat growth and yield.
the development and use of crop models to assess the impact of climatic change on crop growth, and to identify the strategies that can be adopted to reduce the adverse effects of climatic change.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the net effect of increased temperature and CO2 on wheat growth and yield is dependent upon the cultivar used, the ambient CO2 concentration, rainfall and the time of year.
climate change may have significant effects on wheat yield in Victoria, but the magnitude of the effects depends on the cultivar, the ambient CO2 concentration, and the rainfall.
the effects of climate change on wheat growth and production in Victoria, Australia, are highly dependent upon the cultivar, the scenario and the location.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in general, wheat crops grown in the southern part of Victoria are likely to have a higher grain yield under a higher CO2 concentration and a higher ambient temperature.
the potential impact of climate change on crop production in Australia is likely to be less severe than in many other parts of the world.

the potential yield increase due to CO2 enrichment may be offset by the yield loss caused by higher air temperature, especially in the case of the early maturing cultivar, and that the yield increase due to higher rainfall is likely to be offset by the loss due to higher temperature in the case of late maturing cultivars.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use the model to identify the best wheat varieties that are most resilient to climate change.
we should not expect a simple response from wheat growth to increased temperature.
the sensitivity of crop yield to climate change will be highly dependent on the cultivar used, and that there is no single cultivar that will be optimal for all climate change scenarios.
